_comment: Machine-extracted order-membership proposals. UNREVIEWED. Every entry quotes its source. Not merged into data/kg-seeds.json until a human signs off.
_method: Every one of the 169 rows in the shrine corpus was checked: all 52 rows with a silsila value, and every row whose description matched an order-name/silsila keyword sweep (plus a second sweep for less common orders, initiation vocabulary and sect labels). shrine_entries/ (39 files) and entries/ (10 files) were swept the same way. Nothing here comes from model knowledge of these saints or orders; each quote was verified as a verbatim substring of the source named.

_conventions.parentOrder: one of the five existing order slugs, or null when the source does not place the value under one of them
_conventions.parentOrders: set when the source names more than one order for the saint; parentOrder is then null unless one order is primary in the source
_conventions.asRecorded: the raw silsila cell, verbatim, including any caveat text
_conventions.isProseNotValue: true when the cell is a sentence rather than an order name; such cells get NO membership proposal
_conventions.confidence: 0.95 = order named explicitly for this saint, unambiguous. 0.7 = hedged in the source, or stated of the shrine/place/lineage rather than the person, or the branch->parent split is an inference from a compound name.
_conventions.evidence: 'silsila-column' or 'prose'. Where both exist and add different information, both are proposed; where they disagree, both are proposed and the disagreement is recorded in contradictions.

proposals.notes: The prose places him in two of the five orders as well as founding the Rashidi. Both readings are proposed; neither is chosen over the other.

proposals.quote: He is counted within the Chishti order, the *silsila* most closely identified with Punjabi and Indian Sufism
in the Sufi path he was initiated in the Chishti order, taking spiritual allegiance in the line of Khwaja Shamsuddin Sialvi of Sial Sharif

proposals.quote: The khanqah remains an active centre of Naqshbandi devotion, drawing pilgrims especially at its annual *urs*

proposals.notes: The prose names a narrower branch than the column's "Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi". Both recorded; the Qasimiya layer would be lost if flattened.

Qadiri
proposals.notes: Contradicts the existing seed (shams-ali-qalandar -> qalandariyya). See disagreesWithExistingSeed.

proposals.notes: The corpus itself calls this a branch of the Qadiri order, so the parent mapping is stated, not inferred. "Owaisi" is glossed in the same sentence as a mode of initiation (received inwardly, no living master) — not a separate order.

proposals.quote: a revered Qadiri saint of the sixteenth century who did much to spread the Qadiri order in the Punjab
proposals.notes: Contradicts the existing seed (daud-bandagi-kirmani -> chishtiyya). Column and prose both say Qadiri, repeatedly. See disagreesWithExistingSeed.

proposals.quote: It was Meher Ali Shah, tradition says, who told him that his true portion lay in the Suhrawardi order, with Hazrat Ghulam Muhammad Suhrawardi, and bade him take allegiance there — which he did.
Though he carried both the Gilani-Qadiri and the Suhrawardi inheritances, it was the Gilani-Suhrawardi path that he made his own.
his family descent as a Gilani sayyid is traced, through some twenty-three links, to Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad, and his Sufi allegiance, through some nineteen links
proposals.notes: 0.7 and kept separate from the Suhrawardi proposal because the corpus draws the distinction itself: the Qadiri tie is family descent ("the blood and the blessing"), the Suhrawardi tie is initiatic allegiance. Merging them would erase that distinction.

Qadiri
local devotional tradition attaches to him the composite title "Qadiri Suhrawardi," suggesting an affiliation with the same overlapping Sufi orders associated with his brother's shrine nearby
proposals.notes: 0.7: the source hedges twice ("local devotional tradition", "suggesting"), and the corpus says little is independently documented about him. The composite title must stay composite.

proposals.quote: From this master he received his authorisation (khilafat) in the Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi order, becoming a *khalifa-e-mujaz* of Karman Wali Sharif.
proposals.notes: The row also states the branch's own genealogy: "the branch of the Naqshbandi way renewed by the great reformer Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani)" — i.e. the parent mapping is given in the source, not inferred.

proposals.quote: marks the resting place of the man traditionally credited with establishing the *Chishti* order firmly in the city
Hussain belonged, in spirit, to the *Malamatiyya* — the Sufis of the “path of blame,” who deliberately drew the censure of respectable society upon themselves
proposals.notes: parentOrder null: the Malamatiyya is not a branch of any of the five and the corpus does not place it under one. The overview calls him "the great Malamati Sufi" flatly; the History section hedges with "in spirit". See newOrdersNeeded.

proposals.quote: Suhrawardi
proposals.notes: The column is a plain order name for this figure. Note that the prose supports it only at the level of lineage, not personal initiation: "Its saint bore the *Bukhari* lineage ... whose forebears ... spread the *Suhrawardi* devotional tradition across Sindh and the southern Punjab."

proposals.quote: he became the disciple of a Suhrawardi *faqir* remembered as Shah Saidan Sarmast, serving at his master's *khanqah* with great devotion

A Sufi of the *Suhrawardi* order, honoured also with an Uwaisi spiritual lineage, he is remembered as the founder of the *Sarwari* branch of the order in Sindh
he is remembered as the founder of the *Sarwari* branch of the order in Sindh
proposals.notes: IMPORTANT COLLISION: this "Sarwari" is a branch of the SUHRAWARDI order in Sindh, founded by Makhdoom Nooh. It is not the same as Sultan Bahu's "Sarwari Qadiri" (a branch of the Qadiri order). Two distinct branches share a name; they must not be merged into one node.

proposals.quote: an adherent of the Suhrawardi silsila founded by Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan

Qadiri
proposals.notes: The column names only Qadiri; the prose of the same row names two orders. See the prose proposal and contradictions.

a modern Sufi master and the founder of the Azeemia Sufi order
proposals.notes: parentOrder null: the corpus presents the Azeemia as an order he founded in the twentieth century, with no parent among the five. Contradicts the existing seed (qalandar-baba-auliya -> qalandariyya); "Qalandar Baba" is given in the corpus as a spiritual title, not an order. See disagreesWithExistingSeed and newOrdersNeeded.

proposals.quote: He combined the Qadiri and Shattari silsilas in his own practice and authored several Persian works of mystical philosophy
proposals.notes: multiple=true: the source names two silsilas. Only one of them (Qadiri) exists among the five; Shattari has no node, so parentOrders lists only qadiriyya and the Shattari half is carried by the branch string and newOrdersNeeded. Do not read the single parentOrder as the whole of his affiliation.

proposals.saintName: Syed Shah Jamal Uddin Naqvi Bukhari
proposals.quote: The shrine — of the Suhrawardi line and the Ahl-e-Sunnat tradition — has been in the care of the government's Auqaf Department since 1960
proposals.notes: "Ahl-e-Sunnat" in the same sentence is a sect, not an order, and is not proposed as one. The column records only Suhrawardi; the prose records three orders — see the prose proposal and contradictions.

proposals.saintName: Syed Shah Jamal Uddin Naqvi Bukhari
proposals.quote: He belonged jointly to the Qadiriyya, Suhrawardiyya and Chishtiyya orders — a special disciple, tradition holds, of Sheikh Khokar Baig Suhrawardi
proposals.notes: The row also traces his Suhrawardi lineage specifically to Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, on the authority of Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*.

proposals.quote: Learned and devout, he was a shaykh of the Qadiri order and a guide of many disciples
proposals.notes: The row also uses the compound "Qadiri-Gilani" for the family line in Multan ("Through him and his descendants the Qadiri-Gilani presence was firmly established in Multan").

proposals.quote: He was initiated in the Chishti order and became a spiritual heir within the line of Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi
the ancient town in Bahawalpur district that was for centuries a great centre of the Suhrawardi order and of the Bukhari Sayyids
proposals.notes: 0.7: the column gives the order, but the only prose support states it of Uch Sharif as a place, not of this figure. Nothing in the row describes his own initiation or teachers.

proposals.quote: Bibi Jawindi is remembered as a pious woman of the Jalali Bukhari line — by tradition a great-granddaughter of the celebrated saint Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht — venerated for her holiness.
proposals.notes: 0.7: the prose places her in the "Jalali Bukhari line" (a descent group) and never names an order for her; the row's other Suhrawardi mention is about the tomb style of "the Suhrawardi saints". Also note a modelling clash: existing-saints.json attaches this shrine to jalaluddin-surkh-posh-bukhari, not to Bibi Jawindi, who has no saint node.

proposals.saintName: Ghazi Syed Shah Fateh Muhammad Bukhari
proposals.quote: the saint honoured at Wadpagga, Ghazi Baba, belonged to the *Bukhari sayyids*, that widely revered lineage which traces its descent through the great Suhrawardi saints of the medieval Punjab and Sindh
proposals.notes: 0.7: descent through Suhrawardi saints, not a stated initiation. The row's other order sentence lists "Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi" as the movements that took root around Peshawar generally — not as this saint's affiliations, and not proposed as such.

proposals.quote: an inheritance tradition credits him with carrying forward, though he himself is remembered in the *Uwaisi* style of not naming a personal living guide
proposals.notes: 0.7: the column singles out Naqshbandi, but the prose attributes all four orders to his forefathers and marks him Uwaisi — explicitly without a personal living guide. The other three orders are NOT proposed, because the corpus attributes them to the forefathers collectively; and Uwaisi is described as a style, not an order. See contradictions.

proposals.asRecorded: Naqshbandī Mujaddidī (survey answer as written: "Naqshbandi Majdadi - Ahl e Sunnat"; "Ahl e Sunnat" is the sect answer, not a *silsila*)

proposals.notes: Not in the 169-row corpus and not in existing-saints.json — a drafted entry only, so the shrineSlug here is derived from the entry title and is NOT yet a dataset slug. 0.7 because the entry's own qa_note says "SILSILA UNSUPPORTED BY THE BIOGRAPHY ... The silsila field therefore rests on the one-line Q5 answer alone."

branchesFound.reasoning: The corpus names it as an order in its own right and identifies it with the Chishti silsila of Mu'in al-Din Chishti and Nizam al-Din Awliya: "He is counted within the Chishti order, the *silsila* most closely identified with Punjabi and Indian Sufism through its great early masters — Khwaja Mu'in al-Din Chishti of Ajmer and Khwaja Nizam al-Din Awliya of Delhi — and Eidgah Sharif accordingly stands in the Chishti-Nizami current of devotion".

A compound name recorded for one saint; the row also uses "Chishti Nizami Qadria" and "Chishti Qadria order" and names his master "Chishti-Nizami". The two parents are read off the name, not stated in the text, so parentOrder is left null and the compound kept whole.

Appears only inside the name of the saint's murshid, "Hazrat Shah Niyaz Ahmad Chisti Qadri", in a survey answer the entry itself calls not fully grammatical. Kept as recorded; parents inferred from the name only.
Stated in the corpus as a branch of the Naqshbandi order: "the branch of the Naqshbandi way renewed by the great reformer Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani)".

Named as the order resident at Mohra Sharif: "It is the home of the *Naqshbandi Mujaddidi Qasimiya* order". A narrower layer than the column's "Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi"; recorded so it is not flattened away.

The corpus attributes the branch name to Pnina Werbner's fieldwork, "who identifies the tariqa's specific branch name as *tariqa Naqshbandiyya Ghamkolia*", within a shrine it calls a centre of the Naqshbandi order.

Stated as a branch founded by Sultan Bahu after his own Qadiri initiation: "Bahu received initiation in the Qadiri order at the hand of Sayyid Abdul Rahman of Delhi" and "He founded his own branch of the order, the Sarwari Qadiri, which spread widely after him." No membership proposal is made — sultan-bahoo -> qadiriyya is already in the seeds — but the branch is recorded here so it is not lost.

A DIFFERENT Sarwari from Sultan Bahu's: "A Sufi of the *Suhrawardi* order ... he is remembered as the founder of the *Sarwari* branch of the order in Sindh" — here "the order" is the Suhrawardi. Two branches share the name Sarwari under different parents; they must not be merged.

Stated as a branch of the Qadiri order founded by its saint: "the founder of the Naushahia branch of the Qadiri Sufi order" and "He took the Sufi path in the Qadiri order and, attaining a high spiritual station, founded his own branch, the *Naushahia*". No membership proposal — syed-muhammad-noushah-qadiri -> qadiriyya is already seeded.

Parent stated in the source: "he belonged to the *Owaisi Qadiriyya Noshahi* lineage, a branch of the great *Qadiri* order (traced to the twelfth-century saint Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad) as transmitted through the Noshahi Sufis of the Punjab". "Owaisi" is glossed there as inward initiation without a living master — a mode, not an order.

"He combined the Qadiri and Shattari silsilas in his own practice." Qadiri maps to the existing node; Shattari has none (see newOrdersNeeded), so the branch string carries the second half. The row also names his teacher variously "Muhammad Ali Raza Shattari" and "Hazrat Shah Raza Qadri Shattari" and declines to choose between them.

Same branch, different spelling, in another row: Bulleh Shah "became the disciple of Shah Inayat Qadiri, a Sufi master of Lahore of the Qadiri-Shattari line". Recorded because the two spellings refer to the same line and a build should not treat them as two branches by accident.
"a widely revered Sufi master of the Qadiri-Chishti tradition" and "uniting the Qadiri and Chishti lineages" — here the text does state two memberships, not merely a compound name.

"local devotional tradition attaches to him the composite title \"Qadiri Suhrawardi,\" suggesting an affiliation with the same overlapping Sufi orders" — the corpus calls it a composite title and hedges the affiliation.
"it was the Gilani-Suhrawardi path that he made his own" — his Gilani sayyid descent carried into the Suhrawardi allegiance he took at Meher Ali Shah's direction.

"Though he carried both the Gilani-Qadiri and the Suhrawardi inheritances" — in this row the Qadiri side is descent from Abd al-Qadir Jilani rather than initiation. The variant "Qadiri-Gilani" appears in the same row ("an heir to the Qadiri-Gilani and Suhrawardi orders") and in the Syed Musa Pak row ("the Qadiri-Gilani presence was firmly established in Multan").

0.7-grade inference, recorded as a branch rather than a membership: the corpus says of Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, a Suhrawardi saint, that "his descendants and disciples spread the *Jalali* Bukhari line far and wide — a lineage of sayyids", and describes Bibi Jawindi as "a pious woman of the Jalali Bukhari line". The text calls it a lineage of sayyids, so it may be a descent group rather than an initiatic branch; do not promote it to an order without better evidence.

Named as an order founded by its saint ("the founder of the Rashidi Sufi order"), not as a branch of one of the five — although the same row separately calls him "A Qadiri–Naqshbandi saint". Both are proposed; neither is treated as parent of the other. See newOrdersNeeded.
"the founder of the Azeemia Sufi order", founded in the twentieth century and carried on by Khwaja Shamsuddin Azeemi. The corpus gives it no parent order. See newOrdersNeeded.

The corpus describes the Malamatiyya as a temper or way ("the Sufis of the 'path of blame'"), not as a branch of any of the five, and never attaches it to a parent. Recorded as its own node. See newOrdersNeeded.
"He combined the Qadiri and Shattari silsilas in his own practice" — named as a silsila in its own right alongside the Qadiri, with no parent given.

newOrdersNeeded.name: Rashidi
newOrdersNeeded.whyNotABranchOfTheFive: The corpus calls it "the Rashidi Sufi order", founded by Pir Muhammad Rashid Shah himself, and gives it no parent. The same row separately calls him "A Qadiri–Naqshbandi saint", but does not say the Rashidi is a branch of either, so no parent is asserted here. Slug follows the source's own name; the existing five use an -iyya form, so a human should decide the convention (a code-side label question, not a sheet value).

newOrdersNeeded.name: Azeemia
newOrdersNeeded.whyNotABranchOfTheFive: "the founder of the Azeemia Sufi order" — a twentieth-century foundation with no parent named anywhere in the row. Its transmission is given as Qalandar Baba Auliya to Khwaja Shamsuddin Azeemi.

newOrdersNeeded.name: Malamatiyya
newOrdersNeeded.whyNotABranchOfTheFive: The corpus treats the Malamatiyya as a distinct current, "the Sufis of the 'path of blame'", with no parent order. Note the source uses both "Malamati" (the silsila cell, and "the great Malamati Sufi") and "Malamatiyya" (the prose); the proposed name follows the prose form.

newOrdersNeeded.name: Shattari
newOrdersNeeded.whyNotABranchOfTheFive: Named as a silsila in its own right, on a par with the Qadiri, in the one sentence that describes Shah Inayat's practice: "He combined the Qadiri and Shattari silsilas in his own practice." It is a parent-level order in the source, not a Qadiri sub-branch, even though the recorded value "Qadri Shattari" fuses the two.

rejected.candidate: chishtiyya for hazrat-ali-ibn-usman-al-hujwiri (Data Ganj Bakhsh), from data-darbar prose
rejected.reason: The Chishti references in the row are about Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, who kept a retreat at Hujwiri's tomb — "before he founded his order at Ajmer". Nothing places Hujwiri in the order; he is described as carrying "the sober, learned Sufism of Baghdad into the Punjab". Also rejected from the same row: qadiriyya (the Qadiri mention is Mian Mir's) and "Barelvi" (a devotional school, not a Sufi order).

rejected.candidate: suhrawardiyya for the six Bibis, from shrine-of-bibi-pak-daman prose
rejected.reason: The Suhrawardi line is described as DESCENDING from one of them: "Through Bibi Haj, tradition traces a distinguished line of Suhrawardi saints". Their father's line is named separately as "Junaidiya", not Suhrawardi.

rejected.candidate: a "Junaidiya" order node, from shrine-of-bibi-pak-daman prose
rejected.reason: Named once, of the Bibis' father rather than the shrine's principal figure: "Sayyid Ahmad Tokhta Tirmidhi, a sayyid of the Junaidiya Sufi line whose spiritual descent is traced ... back to Imam Zain al-Abideen". One passing mention of a third party's line is too thin to create an order, and no membership can be attached to a figure the archive does not model.

Abdul Qadir Jilani appears as a member of his family's scholarly milieu, not as his order: "a Hasani-Hussaini family of religious scholars that counted Junaid Baghdadi, Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal and Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani among its" number. The row states the affiliation it does have as "its tradition is Syed and Ahl-e-Sunnat" — a sect and a descent claim, not a silsila.

rejected.candidate: qadiriyya for Shah Abul Muali Qadri, from the saint's name and the Jilani material in darbar-abul-muali-qadri
rejected.reason: The silsila cell states outright that no order was given, and the entry's qa_note 1 says "SILSILA ANSWER NOT A SILSILA". The Jilani material is devotional (dreams, a turban) and "He is said to have loved Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani and Mian Mir deeply" — love, not initiation. Deriving the order from the nisba in his name is precisely the prior-driven inference this archive forbids.

Dynastic, not initiatic. entries/entry_malik_ahmad_ayaz.md: "Ghaznavi is a dynastic rather than an initiatic designation, and the account describes political and military service, not spiritual affiliation", and the survey "never calls him a saint or places him in a Sufi lineage of teachers".

rejected.candidate: an "Ahl-e-Sunnat" order node (recurs for shah-jamal, peer-makki, malik-ahmad-ayaz, wasif-ali-wasif, eidgah-sharif)
rejected.reason: A sect, not a silsila, and the sources say so: entry_mian_qurban_ali_shah.md notes the survey answer "mixes a silsila (Naqshbandi Mujaddidi) with a sect (Ahl-e Sunnat)", and entry_malik_ahmad_ayaz.md treats it the same way.

The corpus defines it as a mode of initiation, not an order: "he himself is remembered in the *Uwaisi* style of not naming a personal living guide", and "the epithet *Owaisi* denotes, in Sufi usage, a spiritual initiation received inwardly rather than from a living master". It belongs on a membership as a qualifier, never as a parent order.
Both qalandar mentions are geographic — the pilgrim road to Lal Shahbaz Qalandar at Sehwan — not an affiliation of Syed Shah Sadaruddin Lakyari.

"Qalandar" is part of his name and a description of temperament — "a man who joined the learning of the seminary to the ecstasy of the *qalandar*" — while the row states his allegiance explicitly and only as Suhrawardi. Proposing qalandariyya would contradict the row's own resolution.

"Sarwarias" in that row are his devotees, not an order: "His devotees — the *Sultanias* or *Sarwarias* — carried his banners in seasonal pilgrimages". No order is named for Sakhi Sarwar anywhere in the row.
The keyword match is incidental prose in an anecdote, not an affiliation. Iqbal is a Secular / Memorial-category figure in this archive.

"the order of devotees descended from Bhai Gurdas, the disciple of Guru Gobind Singh" — a Sikh/Nanakpanthi tradition, not a silsila.
